mental.intro: About 23% of U.S. adults, roughly 59 million people, live with a mental illness in a given year, and only about half receive any treatment. Most conditions are common, treatable, and nothing to be ashamed of.
mental.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (NIMH, SAMHSA NSDUH, Mayo Clinic).

items: Anxiety disorders are the most common group, affecting roughly one in five adults each year with worry, panic, or avoidance.
Depression touches about 8% of adults yearly and is the leading cause of disability among working-age people.
Family history matters: having a parent or sibling with a mood or anxiety disorder roughly doubles your own odds.
Trauma, abuse, or neglect in childhood raises lifetime risk for nearly every mental health condition.
Chronic physical illness such as diabetes, heart disease, or chronic pain frequently brings depression or anxiety with it.
Alcohol and drug use can trigger or worsen mood, anxiety, and psychotic symptoms, and often hides an underlying condition.
Major life stressors like job loss, divorce, bereavement, or money trouble are common tipping points.
Poor sleep is both a cause and a symptom; chronic short sleep sharply raises the risk of anxiety and depression.
Loneliness and social isolation carry health risks comparable to smoking and are rising, with over half of adults reporting daily loneliness.
Financial strain and job insecurity are among the top reported sources of stress for American adults.
Heavy social media and screen use is linked to worse mood, attention, and sleep, especially in teens and young adults.
Lack of physical activity and a poor diet are associated with higher rates of depression and low energy.
Stigma and cost keep about half of people with a mental illness from ever seeking care.
Untreated ADHD, learning differences, and burnout often show up as focus problems or irritability.
Protect sleep: aim for 7 to 9 hours, keep a regular schedule, and get daylight early in the day.
Move most days; even 20 to 30 minutes of brisk walking measurably lowers anxiety and depressive symptoms.
Stay connected by scheduling time with friends, family, or community groups each week rather than waiting until you feel like it.
Limit alcohol, avoid recreational drugs, and notice if substance use is becoming a way to cope.
Learn a simple stress skill such as slow breathing, a brief meditation app, or journaling and practice it daily.
Set boundaries on screens and news, especially in the hour before bed.
Talk to your primary care provider early; most practices now screen for depression and anxiety at routine visits.
If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline) any time, day or night.
Talk therapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), is a first-line treatment for anxiety and depression with strong evidence.
Antidepressants such as SSRIs and SNRIs help many people, usually taking 4 to 6 weeks to show full benefit.
Combining therapy with medication generally works better than either alone for moderate to severe conditions.
Telehealth therapy and psychiatry are now widely available and covered by most insurance plans.
Collaborative care, where your primary care office coordinates with a behavioral health specialist, improves outcomes.
For focus and attention problems, a proper ADHD evaluation followed by behavioral strategies and, if needed, medication is effective.
Peer support groups, employer assistance programs (EAPs), and community mental health centers offer low-cost help.
Newer options such as ketamine-based treatments and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) exist for depression that has not responded to standard care.

addictions.intro: In 2024, about 22% of Americans aged 12 and older (63.7 million) used tobacco or vaped nicotine, and roughly one in four used an illicit drug in the past year. Addiction is a treatable medical condition, not a moral failing.
addictions.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (SAMHSA NSDUH 2024, NIDA, NIAAA).

items: Genetics account for roughly half of a person's vulnerability to addiction, so family history is a strong warning sign.
Starting alcohol, nicotine, or drug use as a teenager greatly raises the chance of a lifelong problem because the brain is still developing.
Untreated anxiety, depression, ADHD, or trauma often drives self-medication with alcohol, drugs, or gambling.
Repeated use changes the brain's reward circuits so that the habit continues even when it causes harm.
Easy access and heavy marketing of alcohol, vapes, sports betting apps, and endlessly scrolling feeds make habits hard to break.
Chronic pain and prescribed opioids remain a common path into opioid dependence.
Social environments where heavy drinking or drug use is normal make it much harder to cut back.
Alcohol is the most widely used substance: 46.6% of people 12 and older drank in the past month, and heavy drinking raises cancer, liver, and heart risks.
Cigarettes still cause the most preventable deaths, and 9.6% of people now vape nicotine, including many who never smoked.
Fentanyl in the illicit drug supply drives most overdose deaths; carrying naloxone (Narcan) saves lives.
Online sports betting has been legalized in most states, and problem gambling calls to helplines have risen sharply since.
Marijuana use, reported by 22.3% of people 12 and older, is more potent today and can cause dependence, especially with daily use.
Stress, loneliness, and boredom are the most common triggers for relapse in every kind of addiction.
Screens and games are designed with variable rewards that mimic slot machines and hijack attention and sleep.
Know your limits: U.S. guidelines suggest no more than 2 drinks a day for men and 1 for women, and less is better.
Delay and discourage any use by teens; every year of delayed first use lowers lifetime risk.
Store alcohol, prescription pills, and cannabis products locked and out of reach of children and visitors.
Set money and time limits before gambling or gaming, and use app-level self-exclusion tools.
Treat underlying mood or anxiety problems instead of using substances to manage them.
Build a routine with exercise, sleep, and supportive people, since structure is a strong buffer against relapse.
Track your use honestly for a month; seeing the real number is often the nudge that starts a change.
If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988; for treatment referrals call SAMHSA's helpline at 1-800-662-4357.
Medications for alcohol use disorder (naltrexone, acamprosate) and opioid use disorder (buprenorphine, methadone, naltrexone) cut relapse and death rates substantially.
Nicotine patches or gum combined with varenicline or bupropion roughly double or triple quit rates compared with willpower alone.
Cognitive behavioral therapy and motivational interviewing help people change patterns and handle cravings.
Contingency management, which rewards verified abstinence, is the most effective approach for stimulants like meth and cocaine.
Mutual support groups such as AA, NA, SMART Recovery, and Gamblers Anonymous are free and improve long-term outcomes.
Free state quitlines (1-800-QUIT-NOW) and the National Problem Gambling Helpline (1-800-GAMBLER) offer confidential coaching.
Telehealth addiction care now lets many people start buprenorphine or counseling from home.
Most insurance, including Medicaid and Medicare, must cover addiction treatment on par with other medical care.

depression.intro: About 8% of U.S. adults, roughly 21 million people, have a major depressive episode each year, and rates are highest (about 19%) among 18 to 25 year olds. Only about 6 in 10 get treatment, even though most people improve with care.
depression.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (NIMH, SAMHSA NSDUH, Mayo Clinic).

items: Depression usually comes from a mix of genetics, brain chemistry, and life events rather than a single cause.
A family history of depression roughly doubles or triples your own risk.
Major losses such as a death, divorce, job loss, or serious illness are the most common triggers for a first episode.
Chronic medical conditions including heart disease, diabetes, cancer, stroke, and chronic pain often bring depression with them.
Hormonal shifts after childbirth, around menopause, or with thyroid problems can cause or worsen low mood.
Alcohol and drug use, and some medications like steroids or certain blood pressure drugs, can cause depressive symptoms.
Childhood trauma and ongoing abuse or neglect are strong predictors of depression in adulthood.
Women are diagnosed at about 1.7 times the rate of men (10.3% vs 6.2%), though men are less likely to seek help.
Insomnia and poor sleep both predict and prolong depression; treating sleep often lifts mood.
Loneliness and social isolation, now reported daily by over half of adults, are powerful drivers of low mood.
Physical inactivity and a diet heavy in ultra-processed food are linked to higher depression rates.
Financial strain, job insecurity, and caregiving burden keep stress hormones high for months at a time.
Untreated anxiety is present in about half of people with depression and makes both conditions worse.
Seasonal changes with less daylight trigger winter depression in some people.
Exercise regularly; 30 minutes of moderate activity most days reduces depression risk and is as effective as medication for mild cases.
Keep a steady sleep schedule and get morning daylight, which steadies mood and energy.
Stay connected: make a standing weekly plan with someone you trust even when you do not feel like it.
Limit alcohol, which is a depressant and interferes with sleep and antidepressant medicines.
Learn to notice early signs such as withdrawing, losing interest, or irritability and act before they deepen.
Ask your primary care provider for a depression screen (PHQ-9) at your annual visit; it takes two minutes.
If you have had depression before, a maintenance plan with your provider cuts the chance of a repeat episode.
If you have thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 right away; it is free, confidential, and available 24/7.
Talk therapy, especially CBT, behavioral activation, and interpersonal therapy, is a first-line treatment with lasting benefits.
Antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion, mirtazapine) help most people, typically within 4 to 8 weeks, and should be adjusted if not.
Combining therapy and medication works best for moderate to severe depression.
Collaborative care through your primary care office, with a care manager and psychiatric consultation, roughly doubles response rates.
Esketamine nasal spray and IV ketamine can bring rapid relief for depression that has not responded to two or more medications.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive, insurance-covered option for treatment-resistant depression.
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) remains the most effective treatment for severe or life-threatening depression.
Light therapy, regular exercise, and digital CBT programs are effective add-ons, particularly for mild or seasonal depression.

marital.intro: In 2023 there were about 2.04 million U.S. marriages (6.1 per 1,000 people) and 672,000 divorces (2.4 per 1,000), the lowest divorce rate in decades. A strong close relationship is one of the best predictors of long-term health, while chronic conflict harms it.
marital.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (CDC/NCHS, CDC Social Connection, APA Stress in America 2025).

items: People in supportive partnerships live longer, recover faster from illness, and have lower rates of heart disease and depression.
Chronic relationship conflict raises stress hormones, blood pressure, and inflammation, with effects similar to other major health risks.
About 70% of adults say their closest relationships do not give them enough emotional support, according to APA's 2025 survey.
Marital distress is one of the strongest predictors of depression and heavy drinking in adults.
Children in high-conflict homes show more anxiety, behavior problems, and sleep trouble.
Divorce after age 50, now called gray divorce, has roughly doubled since 1990 and can seriously damage retirement security.
Couples who manage money together and talk about it openly report far less conflict than those who avoid the subject.
Money disagreements are consistently among the top causes of divorce and daily arguments.
Contempt, criticism, defensiveness, and stonewalling during arguments predict breakups more reliably than the topic being argued about.
Work stress, long hours, and caregiving for children or aging parents leave little time or energy for the partnership.
Untreated depression, anxiety, or substance use in either partner strains the relationship and often goes unrecognized.
Phones and screens at the table and in bed crowd out the daily conversation that keeps couples close.
Infidelity, including emotional or online affairs, is a leading cause of separation.
Mismatched expectations about chores, sex, parenting, or in-laws that are never discussed build resentment over years.
Set aside 15 to 20 minutes a day of screen-free conversation about something other than logistics.
Hold a short weekly money and schedule check-in so small issues do not turn into big fights.
Practice repair: a quick apology or humor during an argument matters more than never arguing.
Keep a ratio of roughly five positive interactions for every negative one, a pattern found in stable couples.
Protect shared fun with a regular date or activity, even a walk, and keep it on the calendar.
Get help for your own sleep, stress, mood, or drinking; personal health problems spill into the relationship.
Raise concerns early and gently rather than waiting until you are furious; how a conversation starts predicts how it ends.
If there is physical harm or fear at home, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788.
Couples therapy, especially Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT) and Gottman Method, helps roughly 70% of couples who complete it.
Integrative behavioral couple therapy has strong evidence and is offered by many licensed marriage and family therapists.
Short premarital or relationship education courses (like PREP) reduce later conflict and divorce risk.
Online couples programs and telehealth sessions make help affordable and private for busy families.
Financial counseling or a shared budgeting tool resolves a top source of conflict for many couples.
Treating one partner's depression, anxiety, or substance use frequently improves the relationship on its own.
Discernment counseling helps couples who are unsure whether to stay together make a clear decision in a few sessions.
Mediation and collaborative divorce lower cost and conflict if separation is the right path, especially when children are involved.

sources.t: CDC/NCHS — Provisional number of marriages and divorces, United States 2000-2023
CDC — Social Connection
NIH News in Health — Do Social Ties Affect Our Health?
Austen Riggs Center — APA 2025 Stress in America summary

stress.intro: More than half of U.S. adults report feeling lonely daily, and 94% of highly lonely adults have at least one physical stress symptom such as headaches, fatigue, or muscle tension (APA 2025). Ongoing stress raises the risk of heart disease, poor sleep, depression, and weight gain.
stress.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (APA Stress in America 2025, Mayo Clinic, AHA).

items: Money worries, including debt, inflation, and housing costs, are consistently the top reported source of stress for American adults.
Work pressure, long hours, and job insecurity affect most workers and spill into home life.
Family demands such as parenting, caregiving for aging parents, and relationship conflict are major daily stressors.
Health problems, your own or a loved one's, create both emotional and financial strain.
Loneliness and social disconnection, now reported daily by over half of adults, amplify every other stressor.
Constant news, political division, and social media feeds keep the nervous system on alert.
Major life changes like moving, divorce, job loss, or bereavement are predictable stress spikes.
Chronic stress keeps cortisol and adrenaline high, which raises blood pressure, blood sugar, and inflammation over time.
Stress disrupts sleep, and poor sleep then makes stress harder to handle, creating a cycle.
Many people cope with stress through overeating, alcohol, smoking, or inactivity, which add their own health harms.
Stress is linked to heart attacks, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and worsening of existing heart disease.
Ongoing stress weakens the immune system and worsens digestive problems, headaches, and chronic pain.
Untreated stress often turns into anxiety or depression if it lasts for months.
Lack of control at work and lack of a support network make stress much more damaging.
Move your body most days; regular exercise is one of the most reliable stress relievers and improves sleep.
Protect sleep with a fixed bedtime, a dark cool room, and no screens for the last hour.
Practice a brief relaxation skill daily such as slow breathing, meditation, or a short walk outdoors.
Make a simple budget and an emergency fund plan; a concrete money plan lowers financial stress even before the numbers improve.
Stay connected by reaching out to one person each day, since social support is the strongest buffer against stress.
Set limits on news and social media, and take breaks from your phone during meals and before bed.
Say no to non-essential commitments and break big tasks into small steps to regain a sense of control.
Limit caffeine and alcohol, which both worsen anxiety and sleep.
If stress becomes overwhelming or you have thoughts of self-harm, call or text 988 any time.
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) teaches practical skills for changing stress-driving thoughts and habits and has strong evidence.
Mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR), an 8-week program, lowers stress, anxiety, and blood pressure in clinical trials.
Employee assistance programs (EAPs) offer free, confidential counseling sessions through many employers.
Treating insomnia with CBT-I often reduces daytime stress more than sleeping pills.
Financial counseling, available free through nonprofit credit counselors, directly addresses money stress.
Regular aerobic exercise and yoga have effects on stress comparable to medication for mild to moderate anxiety.
Short-term medication may help when stress has become an anxiety disorder or is disrupting sleep badly; talk to your provider.
Digital CBT and meditation apps are low-cost, evidence-based options for building daily stress skills.

sources.t: APA — Stress in America 2025: A Crisis of Connection (full report)
Austen Riggs Center — APA 2025 Stress in America summary
Mayo Clinic — Chronic stress puts your health at risk
American Heart Association — Chronic stress can cause heart trouble

physical_therapy.intro: About 1 in 4 U.S. adults (24.3%) lives with chronic pain, and physical therapy is one of the best-supported non-drug ways to restore movement and reduce it.
physical_therapy.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (CDC/NCHS, NIH/AHRQ, Mayo Clinic Proceedings).

items: Low back pain is the single most common reason people are referred to physical therapy, affecting most adults at some point.
Osteoarthritis of the knee, hip, and hands stiffens joints and weakens surrounding muscles, limiting daily movement.
Sports and overuse injuries such as sprains, tendinitis, and rotator cuff strains often need guided rehab to heal fully.
Recovery after surgery, including joint replacements and ACL repair, depends on structured exercise to regain range and strength.
Neck pain and headaches from posture, desk work, and whiplash respond well to targeted mobility and strengthening.
Balance problems and falls in older adults are a leading cause of injury that therapy can directly reduce.
Stroke, Parkinson's, and other neurological conditions cause weakness and coordination loss that rehab helps manage.
Sitting for long hours weakens the core and hips, which shifts strain onto the lower back and knees.
Carrying extra body weight adds several pounds of pressure on knee and hip joints with every step.
Skipping warm-ups or increasing training too fast is behind many tendon and muscle injuries.
Fear of movement after an injury leads to stiffness and deconditioning that prolongs pain.
Poor sleep and high stress lower pain thresholds and slow tissue recovery.
Repetitive work tasks and awkward lifting mechanics wear down the same joints day after day.
Delaying care lets a short-term strain turn into a long-term movement problem.
Strength-train major muscle groups at least twice a week to protect joints and spine.
Stand up and move for a few minutes every hour if you sit for work.
Build activity gradually, adding no more than about 10% in distance or load per week.
Lift with your legs, keep loads close to your body, and avoid twisting under weight.
Practice balance exercises like single-leg stands, especially after age 60.
Maintain a healthy weight to cut the load on knees, hips, and back.
Address nagging pain early; a brief evaluation often prevents months of trouble.
Exercise therapy tailored to your condition remains the strongest-evidence treatment for most chronic musculoskeletal pain.
Manual therapy such as joint mobilization and soft-tissue work can ease pain short term when combined with exercise.
Pain neuroscience education helps people understand pain signals and move with less fear.
Most states allow direct access, so you can often see a physical therapist without a referral.
Telehealth and app-guided home programs have expanded, improving adherence between visits.
Clinical guidelines now favor physical therapy and movement over opioids for back, neck, and joint pain.
Dry needling, heat, and taping are used as add-ons, not replacements, for active rehab.

sources.t: CDC/NCHS — Chronic Pain and High-impact Chronic Pain in U.S. Adults, 2023

fitness.intro: Only about half of U.S. adults get the recommended 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, and fewer than 1 in 4 also meet the muscle-strengthening guideline.
fitness.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (CDC, HHS Physical Activity Guidelines).

items: Regular activity lowers the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, and several cancers.
Adults who move regularly sleep better, think more clearly, and report less anxiety and depression.
Strength training preserves muscle and bone, which protects against falls and fractures later in life.
Even modest activity, well below the guideline, measurably reduces the risk of early death.
Fitness makes everyday tasks like stairs, yard work, and carrying groceries easier and safer.
Physical activity helps control blood pressure, blood sugar, and weight over the long term.
Lack of time is the most cited barrier, yet short 10-minute bouts count toward the weekly total.
Starting too hard too fast causes soreness and injury that drive people to quit within weeks.
All-or-nothing thinking turns one missed workout into a month of missed workouts.
Gym cost, travel, and intimidation keep many people from ever starting.
Desk jobs and screen time make sitting the default for most of the day.
Vague goals like 'get in shape' are hard to act on compared with a scheduled plan.
Injury, chronic illness, or pain can make people afraid to move, even when movement helps.
Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly, such as brisk walking, plus strength work twice a week.
Start with 10 to 15 minutes a day and add a few minutes each week rather than jumping to an hour.
Schedule workouts like appointments and tie them to an existing habit, such as after morning coffee.
Pick activities you actually enjoy; enjoyment predicts long-term adherence better than intensity.
Track your sessions with a simple app or calendar; seeing streaks builds motivation.
Exercise with a friend or group, which adds accountability and makes sessions more fun.
Plan for setbacks: if you miss a day, restart the next day without trying to make it up.
Walking remains the most accessible and best-studied activity; 7,000 to 10,000 steps a day brings most benefits.
Resistance training two to three times a week, with bodyweight or bands, is now recommended for all adults.
Short high-intensity intervals deliver cardio gains in less time for people who are already active.
Wearables and phone apps help people set goals, monitor progress, and stay consistent.
Combining aerobic, strength, balance, and flexibility work gives the broadest health payoff.
Older adults benefit from balance training like tai chi, which cuts fall risk substantially.
Breaking up sitting with brief movement every hour improves blood sugar and circulation.

sources.t: CDC — Adult Activity: An Overview

nutrition.intro: Only about 1 in 10 U.S. adults eats enough fruits and vegetables, and diet is a leading driver of heart disease, diabetes, and obesity.
nutrition.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (CDC, HHS/USDA Dietary Guidelines 2025-2030).

items: Poor diet is linked to more deaths in the U.S. than smoking, mainly through heart disease and stroke.
Eating enough fruits, vegetables, and fiber lowers the risk of type 2 diabetes and some cancers.
Good nutrition supports energy, mood, sleep, and healthy aging, not just weight.
Too much sodium raises blood pressure, which nearly half of U.S. adults already have.
Added sugars, mostly from drinks, contribute to weight gain and fatty liver disease.
Children's eating habits are shaped at home, so family meals influence lifelong health.
Ultra-processed foods are cheap, convenient, and engineered to be hard to stop eating.
Busy schedules push people toward takeout and skipped meals followed by overeating.
Confusing and contradictory diet advice online makes many people give up on changing anything.
Sugary drinks, including sodas, energy drinks, and sweetened coffees, add hundreds of hidden calories.
Restrictive crash diets fail within months because they are too hard to sustain.
Limited access to affordable fresh food in some neighborhoods makes healthy choices harder.
Eating while distracted by screens leads to larger portions and less satisfaction.
Fill half your plate with fruits and vegetables, a quarter with protein, and a quarter with whole grains.
Swap sugary drinks for water, sparkling water, or unsweetened tea as the single highest-impact change.
Plan a few simple meals for the week and shop with a list to cut impulse buys.
Keep cut fruit, nuts, and yogurt visible for snacks instead of chips and candy.
Cook at home more often; home meals average fewer calories and less sodium than restaurant food.
Change one habit at a time and keep it for a few weeks before adding the next.
Read labels for sodium and added sugar rather than focusing only on calories.
The 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines emphasize whole foods, protein, and limiting ultra-processed products and added sugars.
Mediterranean and DASH eating patterns have the strongest evidence for heart health and longevity.
Eating 25 to 30 grams of fiber daily from plants improves blood sugar, cholesterol, and gut health.
Adequate protein spread across meals helps preserve muscle, especially when losing weight or aging.
Registered dietitians, often covered by insurance, provide personalized plans that outperform generic diets.
Keeping added sugar under 10% of daily calories and sodium under 2,300 mg remains the standard advice.
Mindful eating, slowing down and noticing fullness, helps people eat less without counting.

weight_loss.intro: About 40% of U.S. adults have obesity, and losing just 5% to 10% of body weight meaningfully improves blood pressure, blood sugar, and joint pain.
weight_loss.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (CDC, Mayo Clinic, WHO, Pew Research).

items: Eating more calories than the body uses over time, often by only a few hundred a day, drives gradual weight gain.
Ultra-processed foods and sugary drinks are calorie-dense and easy to overeat without feeling full.
Sitting most of the day lowers the calories burned and weakens muscle that helps regulate metabolism.
Short or poor sleep raises hunger hormones and cravings for high-calorie food.
Genetics and family history strongly influence appetite, fat storage, and how easily weight comes off.
Some medicines, including certain antidepressants, steroids, and diabetes drugs, cause weight gain.
Conditions such as hypothyroidism, PCOS, and menopause changes make weight harder to manage.
Large restaurant and packaged portions reset what a normal serving looks like.
Stress and emotional eating turn food into a coping tool rather than fuel.
Weekend and holiday overeating can undo a week of careful choices.
Repeated crash dieting slows metabolism and often ends with regaining more weight.
Alcohol adds empty calories and lowers resolve around food.
Neighborhoods without safe places to walk or affordable fresh food make healthy habits harder.
Weight bias and shame discourage people from seeking help from a doctor.
Weigh yourself or check your waist regularly so small gains are caught early.
Replace sugary drinks with water; this alone can cut hundreds of calories a day.
Get 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus two strength sessions to protect muscle.
Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep, which steadies appetite and energy.
Eat mostly whole foods, with vegetables, fruit, beans, and lean protein filling most of the plate.
Cook at home and plate food in the kitchen rather than eating from the package.
Set realistic goals, such as 1 to 2 pounds a week, and track progress with a log or app.
Structured lifestyle programs combining diet, activity, and coaching remain the first step and can produce 5% to 10% loss.
GLP-1 medicines such as semaglutide and tirzepatide produce 15% to 20% average weight loss and are now used by roughly 1 in 8 U.S. adults.
WHO issued its first guideline in 2025 endorsing GLP-1 therapies for adults with obesity alongside lifestyle care.
Bariatric surgery remains the most effective option for severe obesity, with lasting loss of 25% or more.
Reduced-calorie eating patterns work about equally well; the best diet is the one you can keep.
Medication and surgery work best paired with ongoing nutrition, activity, and follow-up to prevent regain.
Insurance coverage for obesity drugs is expanding but uneven, so check your plan and ask about generics or assistance.

cancer.intro: The American Cancer Society projects about 2.1 million new cancer cases and 626,000 cancer deaths in the U.S. in 2026, yet five-year survival has climbed to 70% and nearly half of cancer deaths are considered avoidable.

items: Lung cancer remains the leading cancer killer in the U.S., causing more deaths than colorectal and pancreatic cancers combined.
Worldwide, lung, female breast, and colorectal cancers are the three most commonly diagnosed, at 2.6, 2.4, and 2.0 million cases a year.
About 1 in 5 people will develop cancer in their lifetime; roughly 1 in 9 men and 1 in 13 women will die from it.
Tobacco use is the single largest preventable cause of cancer and drives most lung, throat, and bladder cases.
Colorectal cancer is rising in adults under 50, which is why screening now starts at age 45 for average-risk people.
Inherited gene changes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 account for a minority of cases but sharply raise risk in affected families.
Excess body weight is linked to at least 13 cancer types, including colon, kidney, uterine, and postmenopausal breast cancer.
Alcohol raises risk of mouth, throat, liver, colon, and breast cancer, and risk climbs with every additional daily drink.
Infections such as HPV, hepatitis B and C, and H. pylori cause a meaningful share of cervical, liver, and stomach cancers.
Ultraviolet exposure from sun and tanning beds is the main driver of skin cancers, including melanoma.
Physical inactivity and diets low in fiber and high in processed meat are tied to higher colorectal cancer rates.
Black men have cancer incidence rates about 78% higher than Asian American and Pacific Islander men, reflecting care and access gaps.
Delayed screening and late-stage diagnosis, not just biology, explain much of the survival gap between communities.
Do not smoke or vape, and if you do, ask your doctor about quit medications, which double your odds of success.
Keep up with screening: colonoscopy or stool tests from 45, mammograms from 40, cervical tests from 21, lung CT if you smoked heavily.
Get the HPV vaccine for kids and young adults through age 26, and the hepatitis B vaccine if you have not had it.
Limit alcohol to one drink a day or less for women and two for men, or skip it entirely.
Aim for a healthy weight with mostly plants, whole grains, and lean protein, and limit processed and red meat.
Get at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, which lowers risk of several common cancers.
Use sunscreen, hats, and shade, and avoid tanning beds completely.
Know your family history and ask about genetic counseling if close relatives had cancer young or multiple cancers.
Surgery remains the first-line cure for many solid tumors caught early, often combined with radiation or chemotherapy.
Immunotherapy drugs that unlock the immune system have lifted survival in metastatic lung cancer from 2% to 10% in two decades.
Targeted therapies match drugs to specific tumor gene mutations, so tumor genomic testing is now routine for many cancers.
Myeloma survival has roughly doubled, from 32% to 62%, thanks to newer drug combinations and cell-based therapies.
Precision radiation such as proton beam and stereotactic techniques deliver higher doses with less damage to healthy tissue.
CAR-T cell therapy, which reprograms a patient's own immune cells, is now approved for several blood cancers.
Clinical trials offer access to next-generation treatments; ask your oncologist whether one fits your diagnosis.
Palliative and supportive care alongside treatment improves quality of life and, in some studies, survival.

sources.t: American Cancer Society — Cancer Facts & Figures 2026
American Cancer Society — Global Cancer Statistics 2026 press release
OncLive — Latest ACS Cancer Statistics Report

nerve.intro: Peripheral neuropathy affects millions of Americans, and diabetes is the leading cause: about two-thirds of people with diabetes develop some degree of nerve damage.
nerve.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (NINDS, Cleveland Clinic, Harvard Health).

items: Diabetes is the number one cause of peripheral neuropathy, with high blood sugar slowly damaging the small nerves in feet and hands.
Physical injury and pressure, from car accidents to repetitive motion like carpal tunnel, can crush or stretch nerves.
Autoimmune diseases such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and Guillain-Barre syndrome attack nerve tissue directly.
Chemotherapy and some HIV, heart, and blood-pressure drugs are common medication causes of nerve damage.
Infections including shingles, Lyme disease, HIV, and hepatitis C can inflame or destroy nerve fibers.
Vitamin B12 deficiency and heavy alcohol use starve nerves of what they need to repair themselves.
Inherited conditions like Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease cause progressive nerve disease from a young age.
Poorly controlled blood sugar over years is the biggest modifiable driver of nerve damage.
Kidney and liver disease allow toxins to build up in the blood that injure nerves.
Heavy drinking both poisons nerves and crowds out nutrients like thiamine and B12.
Exposure to industrial chemicals, heavy metals, or solvents can trigger toxic neuropathy.
Obesity and a sedentary lifestyle raise neuropathy risk even in people without diabetes.
Smoking narrows the blood vessels that feed nerves, worsening damage and slowing healing.
Long-term use of some acid-reducing drugs and metformin can lower B12 and contribute to neuropathy.
Keep blood sugar in your target range; tight control can prevent or delay diabetic neuropathy.
Get the shingles vaccine at 50 or older, since shingles is a common cause of lasting nerve pain.
Limit alcohol to moderate levels or stop entirely if you already have nerve symptoms.
Ask your doctor to check B12 levels if you are vegan, over 60, or take metformin or acid reducers.
Exercise regularly and maintain a healthy weight to improve blood flow to nerves.
Inspect your feet daily if you have diabetes or numbness, and wear well-fitting shoes to prevent unnoticed injuries.
Use ergonomic tools and take breaks from repetitive tasks to avoid pressure neuropathies.
Minimize contact with toxic chemicals at work and home, and use protective gear when you cannot.
Treating the underlying cause, such as lowering blood sugar or replacing B12, can stop and sometimes reverse damage.
Duloxetine, gabapentin, and pregabalin are first-line prescription drugs for nerve pain.
Topical options like lidocaine patches and capsaicin cream can ease localized burning or tingling.
Immunoglobulin therapy and other immune treatments help autoimmune neuropathies such as CIDP.
Physical therapy, braces, splints, and orthopedic shoes improve balance and protect weak or numb limbs.
TENS units, acupuncture, and massage provide relief for some people alongside medical care.
Surgery can relieve trapped nerves, as in carpal tunnel syndrome, when conservative care fails.
Newer disease-specific drugs exist for rare inherited neuropathies, so an accurate diagnosis matters.

sources.t: NINDS — Peripheral Neuropathy
Cleveland Clinic — Peripheral Neuropathy: What It Is, Symptoms & Treatment
Harvard Health — Peripheral neuropathy: Causes, symptoms, treatment, and prevention

bone.intro: About 54 million U.S. adults have doctor-diagnosed arthritis, and nearly 19% of women and 4% of men over 50 have osteoporosis of the hip or spine.

items: Osteoarthritis, the wear-and-tear form, is by far the most common arthritis and mainly affects knees, hips, hands, and spine.
Osteoporosis happens when bone is broken down faster than it is rebuilt, leaving bones porous and easy to fracture.
Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease where the body attacks its own joint linings, often starting in the hands and feet.
Gout is caused by uric acid crystals in joints and is closely tied to diet, alcohol, and kidney function.
Menopause sharply speeds bone loss because estrogen helps keep bone density stable.
Old joint injuries from sports or work commonly turn into arthritis in that joint years later.
Long-term steroid use and some cancer and seizure drugs thin bones as a side effect.
Excess body weight multiplies the load on knees and hips and raises osteoarthritis risk substantially.
A diet low in calcium and vitamin D leaves the body without raw materials to maintain bone.
Sitting most of the day weakens bones, since bone only strengthens when it bears weight.
Smoking and heavy drinking both reduce bone density and slow healing after fractures.
Being female, older, small-framed, white or Asian, or having a parent who broke a hip all raise osteoporosis risk.
Conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, celiac disease, and HIV interfere with bone health.
Repetitive motions at work, like kneeling, lifting, or squatting, wear down specific joints over time.
Do weight-bearing exercise like walking, stair climbing, or dancing most days, plus strength training twice a week.
Get enough calcium (1,000 to 1,200 mg daily) and vitamin D, from food first and supplements if needed.
Keep a healthy weight; losing even 10 pounds takes about 40 pounds of pressure off your knees.
Quit smoking and limit alcohol to protect bone density.
Ask about a bone density (DXA) scan at 65 for women, 70 for men, or earlier if you have risk factors.
Protect joints by using proper lifting form, supportive shoes, and braces during high-impact activity.
Fall-proof your home with good lighting, grab bars, and cleared floors, since falls cause most osteoporotic fractures.
See a doctor early for persistent joint pain or swelling; early treatment slows joint damage.
Bisphosphonates such as alendronate are first-line osteoporosis drugs and cut hip and spine fracture risk significantly.
Denosumab injections and bone-building drugs like teriparatide or romosozumab are options for high fracture risk.
For osteoarthritis, exercise, weight loss, and physical therapy are the most effective first treatments.
Over-the-counter acetaminophen or NSAIDs, plus topical gels, manage osteoarthritis pain for most people.
Rheumatoid arthritis is treated with disease-modifying drugs like methotrexate and biologics that prevent joint destruction.
Gout is controlled with uric-acid-lowering drugs such as allopurinol plus flare medication.
Steroid or hyaluronic acid joint injections can give months of relief for a painful knee or hip.
Joint replacement surgery is highly successful when pain and stiffness no longer respond to other care.

sources.t: CDC — Arthritis Basics
CDC — FastStats: Osteoporosis
NIAMS — Osteoporosis Causes, Risk Factors, & Symptoms
National Institute on Aging — Osteoporosis

muscle.intro: Muscle disease ranges from age-related muscle loss (sarcopenia), which affects roughly 5 to 13% of adults over 60 and up to half of those over 80, to inherited and autoimmune myopathies that cause true muscle weakness.
muscle.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (NIH/NCBI StatPearls, Cleveland Clinic, Mount Sinai).

items: Sarcopenia, the gradual loss of muscle mass and strength with age, is the most common muscle condition in adults.
Inflammatory myopathies such as polymyositis and dermatomyositis occur when the immune system attacks muscle fibers.
Muscular dystrophies like Duchenne and myotonic dystrophy are inherited diseases that progressively weaken muscle.
Statin cholesterol drugs and corticosteroids are the most common medication causes of muscle pain and weakness.
Thyroid disorders and other hormone problems can cause endocrine myopathy that improves when the gland is treated.
Chronic overuse and repetitive strain injure muscles and tendons, especially with poor posture or technique.
Critical illness, long ICU stays, and prolonged bed rest cause rapid muscle wasting.
Sedentary living is the single biggest driver of muscle loss; muscle that is not used is steadily broken down.
Eating too little protein, common in older adults, leaves the body unable to rebuild muscle.
Obesity and insulin resistance blunt the muscle-building response to food and exercise.
Chronic diseases like COPD, heart failure, kidney disease, diabetes, and cancer all accelerate muscle wasting.
Declining testosterone, growth hormone, and IGF-1 with age reduce the body's ability to maintain muscle.
Vitamin D deficiency is linked to weaker muscles and more falls.
Heavy alcohol use directly damages muscle tissue and worsens nutrition.
Strength train all major muscle groups at least twice a week; it is the most proven way to prevent and reverse sarcopenia.
Aim for 20 to 35 grams of protein at each meal, or about 1.0 to 1.2 grams per kilogram of body weight daily.
Stay active every day with walking, stairs, or chores; even light movement slows muscle loss.
Warm up, build intensity gradually, and vary your workouts to avoid chronic strain and overuse injuries.
Check vitamin D levels and supplement if low, especially in winter or if you are mostly indoors.
Tell your doctor about new muscle pain or weakness after starting a statin or other drug; dose changes often help.
Keep chronic conditions like diabetes and thyroid disease well controlled to protect muscle.
Limit alcohol and avoid long stretches of bed rest during illness when your care team allows.
Resistance exercise combined with adequate protein is the core treatment for sarcopenia; no approved drug exists yet.
Inflammatory myopathies are treated with corticosteroids and immune-suppressing drugs, and sometimes IV immunoglobulin.
Stopping or switching the offending medication usually resolves statin- or steroid-related myopathy.
Physical and occupational therapy maintain strength, mobility, and independence across nearly all muscle diseases.
Duchenne muscular dystrophy now has targeted drugs, including exon-skipping and gene therapies, that slow progression.
Treating the underlying cause, such as a thyroid disorder or electrolyte imbalance, reverses many acquired myopathies.
Braces, mobility aids, and breathing support help people with advanced muscular dystrophy stay active and safe.
Genetic testing and specialist neuromuscular clinics give faster, more accurate diagnosis and access to trials.

sources.t: NIH/NCBI StatPearls — Sarcopenia
NIH/NCBI StatPearls — Myopathy
Cleveland Clinic — Myopathy: Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis & Treatment
Mount Sinai — Myopathy Diagnosis & Treatments

allergies.intro: Nearly one in three U.S. adults has a seasonal allergy, eczema, or food allergy, with seasonal allergies alone affecting 25.7% of adults and food allergies 6.2%.
allergies.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (CDC NCHS, ACAAI, FARE).

items: Pollen from trees, grasses, and weeds is the leading trigger of seasonal allergies (hay fever) from spring through fall.
Dust mites, pet dander, mold, and cockroaches cause year-round indoor allergies.
Nine foods cause most food allergies: milk, eggs, peanuts, tree nuts, soy, wheat, fish, shellfish, and sesame.
Insect stings from bees, wasps, and fire ants can cause severe, even life-threatening reactions.
Medications such as penicillin and NSAIDs are common causes of drug allergy.
Latex and skin contact with metals like nickel or fragrances cause contact allergies.
Allergies happen when the immune system mistakes a harmless substance for a threat and releases histamine.
Family history is the strongest predictor; a child with two allergic parents has a much higher chance of allergies.
Longer, warmer pollen seasons driven by climate change are raising pollen counts and symptom severity.
Early childhood environments with less microbial exposure appear to increase allergy risk later.
Having one allergic condition, like eczema or asthma, raises the odds of developing others.
Air pollution and tobacco smoke irritate airways and make allergic reactions worse.
Women report higher rates of seasonal, food, and skin allergies than men.
Adults can develop new allergies at any age, often after moving, a new pet, or a major illness.
Introduce peanut and egg to infants early, around 4 to 6 months, which cuts the risk of food allergy substantially.
Check daily pollen counts and keep windows closed and use air conditioning on high-pollen days.
Shower and change clothes after time outdoors to wash pollen off skin and hair.
Use allergen-proof mattress and pillow covers and wash bedding weekly in hot water to control dust mites.
Run a HEPA air purifier and vacuum with a HEPA filter, especially if you have pets.
Fix leaks and keep indoor humidity under 50% to prevent mold growth.
Read food labels every time and tell restaurants about food allergies; carry epinephrine if prescribed.
Get tested by an allergist to identify exact triggers instead of guessing.
Non-drowsy antihistamines like cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine are first-line for sneezing, itching, and runny nose.
Steroid nasal sprays such as fluticasone are the most effective single treatment for nasal allergy symptoms.
Allergy shots (immunotherapy) reduce hay fever symptoms in about 85% of people and can provide lasting relief.
Under-the-tongue tablets now offer immunotherapy at home for grass, ragweed, and dust mite allergies.
Epinephrine auto-injectors are the only treatment for anaphylaxis; a needle-free nasal spray version is now available.
Oral immunotherapy and the injectable drug omalizumab can reduce the severity of reactions to peanut and other foods.
Antihistamine eye drops and saline nasal rinses ease itchy eyes and congestion with few side effects.
Biologic drugs like dupilumab treat severe eczema and asthma that do not respond to standard care.

prevention.intro: Preventive care means catching problems early or avoiding them altogether through screenings, vaccines, and daily habits. CDC notes that more than one in four adults 65 and older falls each year, yet fewer than half tell their doctor, a reminder that many risks go unmentioned until a checkup asks.

items: Regular checkups combine a physical exam, screening tests, vaccines, dental cleanings, and counseling on habits like diet, exercise, and tobacco.
Screenings look for disease before symptoms appear, such as blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, and several common cancers.
Vaccines for flu, COVID-19, shingles, pneumonia, and tetanus keep immunity current because protection from childhood shots fades over time.
A written family health history, including conditions and ages at diagnosis, helps your doctor decide which screenings you need earlier.
Most preventive services recommended by the USPSTF are covered without copay by insurance plans under the Affordable Care Act.
Dental and eye exams are part of prevention too, catching gum disease, glaucoma, and diabetes-related eye changes early.
Mental health check-ins, including depression screening at routine visits, are now standard preventive care for adults and teens.
High blood pressure usually has no symptoms but drives heart attacks, strokes, and kidney failure; a simple cuff reading finds it.
High cholesterol and prediabetes are silent for years; a blood test can reveal them before arteries or organs are damaged.
Colorectal cancer screening finds precancerous polyps that can be removed before they ever become cancer.
Breast cancer found on a mammogram is typically smaller and easier to treat than one found as a lump.
Cervical cancer is largely preventable through HPV vaccination plus Pap and HPV testing.
Lung cancer screening with a low-dose CT scan is recommended for adults 50 to 80 with a heavy smoking history.
Falls in older adults, the leading cause of traumatic brain injury, can be predicted by a quick balance and medication review.
Hepatitis C and HIV can be carried for years unnoticed; one-time testing is recommended for most adults.
In your 20s and 30s: blood pressure at every visit, cholesterol every 4 to 6 years, cervical screening from 21, and HPV vaccine if not done.
From age 35 to 40: blood sugar testing if overweight, and start discussing mammogram timing with your doctor.
From age 40: mammograms every one to two years for women; cholesterol and diabetes checks become routine.
From age 45: colorectal cancer screening begins, by colonoscopy every 10 years or a stool test every 1 to 3 years.
From age 50: lung cancer CT if you have a 20 pack-year smoking history, shingles vaccine, and prostate cancer discussion for men.
From age 65: bone density scan for women, pneumonia vaccine, annual fall-risk check, and a one-time abdominal aneurysm ultrasound for men who ever smoked.
At every age: flu shot yearly, COVID-19 vaccine as advised, tetanus booster every 10 years, and dental cleaning twice a year.
Not smoking, or quitting, is the single largest preventable reduction in cancer, heart disease, and lung disease risk.
At least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity plus two strength sessions lowers risk of heart disease, diabetes, and falls.
A diet built on vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, and fish, with little processed meat and sugar, protects heart and gut.
Keeping alcohol to no more than one drink a day for women or two for men reduces cancer, liver, and injury risk.
Seven to nine hours of sleep a night supports blood pressure, blood sugar, mood, and immune function.
Keeping a healthy weight and waist size cuts the risk of diabetes, several cancers, and joint problems.
Wearing a seat belt, a bike helmet, and sunscreen are cheap, proven habits that prevent common injuries and skin cancer.
Bring a list of questions and medications to each checkup so nothing gets missed and your doctor can tailor screenings.

postop.intro: Recovering from an operation is a gradual process that depends on the type of surgery, the anesthesia used, and your health going in. Most surgical wound infections show up within 30 days, which is why the first month of aftercare matters most.
postop.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (Mayo Clinic Health System, MedlinePlus).

items: Right after surgery you are monitored in a recovery room for vital signs, pain, and nausea until the anesthesia wears off enough to move on.
Pain is managed with a plan that usually combines non-opioid medicines, short opioid use if needed, ice, and positioning.
Wounds heal in stages over weeks: early swelling and redness, then new tissue, then a scar that keeps strengthening for months.
Early walking, deep breathing, and coughing exercises lower the risk of blood clots and pneumonia in the first days.
Follow-up visits check the incision, remove stitches or staples, review medicines, and clear you for more activity.
Energy and appetite often lag for weeks; fatigue is normal and is not a sign that something has gone wrong.
Physical or occupational therapy is common after joint, spine, heart, and abdominal surgery and speeds the return to normal function.
Smoking narrows blood vessels, starves the wound of oxygen, and roughly doubles the risk of wound complications.
Poorly controlled diabetes, obesity, and a weakened immune system all raise the chance of surgical site infection.
Taking steroids such as prednisone, or having an operation that lasts longer than two hours, increases infection risk.
Doing too much too soon can reopen an incision or cause a hernia; doing too little raises clot and pneumonia risk.
Poor nutrition, especially low protein, slows tissue repair; alcohol interferes with healing and pain medicine.
Skipping prescribed blood thinners, antibiotics, or breathing exercises is a leading reason for readmission.
Signs of trouble to report right away: fever, pus or bad smell from the wound, spreading redness, calf pain, or shortness of breath.
Attend every pre-op appointment and class; the pre-surgical exam checks medicines, history, and whether you are fit for anesthesia.
Stop smoking as early as possible, ideally four or more weeks before, and avoid alcohol in the days leading up.
Bring a current list of all medicines and supplements, allergies, your insurance card, and any advance directive.
Ask which medicines to pause, such as blood thinners or diabetes drugs, and follow the fasting instructions exactly.
Eat well, stay hydrated, and sleep enough in the week before; walking daily builds the reserve you will draw on afterward.
Arrange a ride home and someone to stay with you for the first 24 hours after general anesthesia.
Set up your home in advance: clear walkways, put essentials at waist height, stock easy meals, and prepare a sleeping spot you can get in and out of.
Write down your surgeon's phone number and the symptoms that should trigger a call or a trip to the emergency department.
Follow the discharge instructions on wound care, bathing, lifting limits, and driving; they are specific to your operation.
Wash your hands before touching the incision, keep the dressing clean and dry, and change it exactly as instructed.
Take pain medicine on schedule at first so you can move, breathe deeply, and sleep; taper as the pain eases.
Walk a little several times a day and increase gradually; movement is the single best tool against clots and constipation.
Eat protein at each meal, drink plenty of fluids, and use fiber or a stool softener if opioids slow your bowels.
Accept help from family and friends with meals, chores, and rides rather than pushing through alone.
Keep every follow-up visit and therapy session, and ask before restarting any medicine or activity you are unsure about.
Call your surgeon promptly about fever, wound drainage, rising pain, leg swelling, or chest symptoms; early treatment prevents serious complications.

accident.intro: Unintentional injuries are a leading cause of death for Americans under 45, driven mainly by drug poisonings, falls, and vehicle crashes. NHTSA estimates 36,640 people died on U.S. roads in 2025, the lowest since 2019, while the CDC reports unintentional fall deaths have nearly doubled since 2003.

items: Unintentional drug overdose is the largest injury killer, at about 29 deaths per 100,000 people in 2023, mostly from fentanyl-laced supply.
Falls kill about 11 per 100,000 Americans a year and send roughly 3 million older adults to emergency departments.
Motor vehicle crashes caused about 12.5 deaths per 100,000 in 2023; 2025 saw an estimated 36,640 traffic deaths nationwide.
Falls are the leading cause of traumatic brain injury and cause about 319,000 hip fracture hospitalizations among older adults each year.
Home hazards such as burns, scalds, and kitchen cuts are among the most common reasons for urgent care visits.
Drowning is a leading cause of death for children ages 1 to 4, usually in backyard pools or bathtubs.
Workplace injuries cluster in construction, transportation, agriculture, and warehousing, led by falls, struck-by, and vehicle incidents.
Alcohol or drugs are involved in a large share of crashes, falls, drownings, and fires; impairment multiplies every other risk.
Distraction, especially phone use, injures 18 people every half hour on U.S. roads according to NHTSA.
Speeding, not wearing a seat belt, and drowsy driving are consistently the top factors in fatal crashes.
Older age, muscle weakness, poor balance, vision loss, and medicines that cause dizziness raise fall risk; one fall doubles the chance of another.
Clutter, loose rugs, poor lighting, and no grab bars turn ordinary homes into fall hazards.
Fatigue, rushing, and skipping protective gear are behind many work and home tool injuries.
Fewer than half of older adults who fall tell their doctor, so risks go unaddressed until a serious injury.
Buckle up every trip, keep to the speed limit, put the phone away, and never drive after drinking or when drowsy.
Use correctly installed car seats and boosters for children and insist teens follow graduated licensing rules.
Remove trip hazards, add night lights, install grab bars and stair rails, and wear supportive shoes indoors.
Do strength and balance exercise like tai chi, get eyes checked yearly, and ask a doctor to review medicines that cause dizziness.
Keep medicines, including opioids, locked away; carry naloxone if anyone in the household uses opioids or buys pills outside a pharmacy.
Install smoke and carbon monoxide alarms on every level, test them monthly, and keep a fire extinguisher near the kitchen.
Fence pools, never leave young children alone near water, and wear life jackets while boating.
Wear helmets, eye protection, gloves, and sturdy footwear for bikes, ladders, power tools, and yard work.

sections.t: What to do after an injury
items: Call 911 for head injury with confusion, heavy bleeding, trouble breathing, chest pain, suspected overdose, or inability to move a limb.
For a suspected overdose, give naloxone if available, call 911, and stay with the person until help arrives.
Stop bleeding with firm direct pressure, and do not move someone with a possible neck or back injury unless they are in danger.
For sprains and strains use rest, ice, compression, and elevation, and seek care if you cannot bear weight or the joint looks deformed.
After any fall, even without obvious injury, tell your doctor; it triggers a fall-risk review that can prevent the next one.
Cool burns under running water for 20 minutes, cover loosely, and seek care for large, deep, or facial burns.
Report workplace injuries the same day and document the incident; it protects both your health and your benefits.
Keep a first aid kit, emergency numbers, and a list of medicines where everyone in the household can find them.

heart.intro: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in the US — about one in three deaths — and coronary artery disease is its most common form. Most of the risk is driven by a handful of measurable, changeable things.
heart.updated: Sources checked August 2026 (CDC; 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline).

items: Coronary artery disease — plaque (cholesterol and inflammation) narrowing the arteries that feed the heart; the most common form and the usual cause of heart attacks.
High blood pressure — years of extra pressure thicken and stiffen the heart and arteries and can lead to heart failure.
Arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation — irregular rhythm that raises stroke risk and can weaken the heart over time.
Heart failure — the heart can’t pump well enough, usually the end result of the causes above.
Valve disease and cardiomyopathy — damaged valves or heart muscle, sometimes inherited, sometimes from infection or long-term strain.
The “big three” the CDC names: high blood pressure, high cholesterol (especially LDL), and smoking — roughly half of US adults have at least one.
Diabetes and insulin resistance — high blood sugar damages blood-vessel walls.
Excess weight, especially around the middle, and physical inactivity.
Diet high in saturated fat, salt, and added sugar; excessive alcohol.
Family history and genetics — including lipoprotein(a), an inherited cholesterol particle the 2026 guideline now says every adult should have measured at least once.
Chronic stress, poor sleep, and untreated sleep apnea.
Age, and for women the years after menopause.
Know your numbers: blood pressure, cholesterol (cholesterol checked every 4–6 years, more often if at risk), blood sugar, and weight. Ask about the newer PREVENT risk score.
Move: at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity (a brisk walk counts), plus two days of strength work.
Eat for your arteries: vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, nuts, fish; less processed food, saturated fat, salt, and sugar.
Don’t smoke or vape — quitting cuts heart-disease risk within a year.
Keep alcohol modest and sleep 7–9 hours.
If you have high blood pressure, cholesterol, or diabetes, take the medicines you’ve been prescribed — consistency matters more than perfection.
Learn the warning signs of a heart attack (chest pressure, shortness of breath, pain spreading to the arm, jaw, or back, cold sweat, nausea) and call 911 — don’t drive yourself.
Lifestyle change is first-line at every stage — it’s the foundation every treatment below builds on.

Cholesterol: statins remain first-line; ezetimibe is added when a statin alone isn’t enough; PCSK9 inhibitors (injectables), bempedoic acid, and inclisiran are the next steps. The 2026 guideline sets lower LDL targets for higher-risk people (under 70, and under 55 for the highest risk).
Blood pressure: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, calcium-channel blockers, and thiazide diuretics — often two together at low doses.
Blood sugar and weight: SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 medicines (such as semaglutide) now carry proven heart-protection benefits beyond their original uses.
Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor) and anticoagulants for people with existing disease or atrial fibrillation — no longer routine aspirin for prevention in healthy adults.
Procedures: stents (PCI) and bypass surgery (CABG) for significant blockages; catheter-based valve replacement (TAVR) and ablation for rhythm problems.
Heart failure: the “four pillars” — ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor — plus devices such as ICDs and cardiac resynchronization when needed.
Cardiac rehab after a heart event — supervised exercise and education that measurably lowers the chance of a second one.
